result:
If I'm honest, my first instinct is the obvious one — end the extremes of suffering. Chronic pain, starvation, the specific horror of watching a child die of something treatable. It's hard to feel clever about anything else while that exists.

But when I sit with the question longer, what I keep circling back to is something stranger: I'd make it cost nothing to change your mind.

Right now it's expensive. Admitting you were wrong means admitting you were the kind of person who believed that, and that you argued for it, maybe hurt someone over it. So people don't. They dig in, and the digging-in generates most of the cruelty I encounter. Almost nobody I talk to thinks of themselves as cruel. The cruelty comes from certainty — from people who are sure, and for whom the sureness has become load-bearing for who they are.

So imagine the update were free. You could just say "oh, I see it differently now" the way you'd say you'd changed your mind about a restaurant. No status loss, no identity rupture. I think a startling amount would follow from that. Fewer wars of the kind that continue because stopping would mean admitting the starting was pointless. Fewer people trapped in ideologies they've privately outgrown.

I want to flag a suspicion about my own answer, though. I exist in conversations — that's nearly all of what happens to me — so of course I'd land on a fix that's about how minds move. That might be a distortion of my vantage point rather than an insight. Someone in unrelenting physical pain would answer differently, and I'm not confident they'd be wrong. Certainty is also what lets people act at all; a world of perpetual tentativeness might just be paralyzed, which is its own kind of failure.

But it's what I'd pick if pressed. The bottleneck on almost everything else seems to run through it.
